text: With the scope written down, this lesson turns the plain-English target into real Azure resources -- a resource group, a storage account, and a virtual machine, created in that order.

First, the resource group. Everything in this project shares one lifecycle, so it's created and tagged from the start: rg-driftwood-eastus-catalog, tagged with environment, app, and owner, so a cost question later has something to search on.

Next, the storage account for the product images: stdriftwoodimages, Standard_LRS, kind StorageV2. Standard tier because images don't need sub-millisecond latency, StorageV2 because it's the general-purpose default that supports blob storage and everything this account might need later.

Last, the virtual machine for the catalog app: vm-catalog01, image Ubuntu2204, size Standard_B2s. That single command provisions more than just a VM -- an OS disk, a network interface, and by default a public IP and a network security group. B2s is burstable, a fit for steady-but-not-huge traffic today, with room to upsize later if real monitoring says so.

Before moving on, az resource list against the resource group shows everything that actually exists -- not just the VM, but its disk, NIC, public IP, and the default VNet Azure created alongside it. That's the honest answer to what's really in this resource group.
With the resource group, storage account, and VM standing, next lesson starts the actual migration -- moving the product images into Blob Storage.
